title: We cannot but speak (Acts 4:1–22)
hookLine: unlearned fishermen before the council, and people realize they'd been with Jesus
tomorrow: a man sells a field and gets a nickname. what does it mean?

cards: Spend a summer with a friend and you come home using her phrases without noticing. Acts 4 has a stranger version of that.

Peter and John are arrested and stood before the council, then ordered never to speak in Jesus' name again. Their answer is why they can't stop: "we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard."
But here's the odd detail. Before that, the council has already worked something out about them: "they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus." How could they tell?

teach.b: Acts leaves three clues. Clue one: "when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled."

Unlearned and ignorant isn't a verdict on their minds here; it means they hadn't trained the way the council's scholars had. Fishermen, as the Gospels tell it. Plain men speaking like that had learned it somewhere.

teach.h: CLUE TWO: THE STONE THE BUILDERS SKIPPED.
teach.b: Peter reaches for a psalm about "the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner," the same psalm line Jesus quotes in Matthew. They talk like the one they'd been with.

teach.h: CLUE THREE: THE MAN STANDING THERE.
teach.b: Clue three is the loudest, and it says nothing at all: "beholding the man which was healed standing with them, they could say nothing against it." Standing. He used to be carried to the gate.
So the answer: it showed in their nerve, in their words, and in the person standing beside them.
Then the order to be silent, and the reply, which doesn't shout: "Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye."
One to tell a friend tonight: the Greek word for their boldness, parrhesia, means open, frank speech, saying it plainly.

how: Some Christians pray for boldness in the words of Acts 4, and the line 'we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard' is quoted in some churches when people tell their own stories of faith.

games.q: what does “we cannot but speak” mean?
o: we won't argue, so we'll stay silent now
we can't keep quiet about what we've seen
we're no longer permitted to speak at all

games.q: before the council — tap the pairs.
p: the stone the builders set at nought
the question handed back to the council

s: Peter and John answer the council with an angry speech
they hand the question back: whether it be right in the sight of God… judge ye.
Peter and John agree to stop speaking in Jesus' name
for we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.
the council had nothing to say while the healed man stood there
beholding the man which was healed standing with them, they could say nothing against it.

games.q: your new manager notices you stay calm when customers yell, and asks where you learned it. honestly, it was your grandmother. what fits Acts 4?
o: tell her plainly: you learned it from your grandmother.
say you've just always been calm by nature.
change the subject; it's too personal for work.
games.why: the council could tell Peter and John had been with Jesus. what we carry shows where we've been, and honesty can simply say so.

practice: Sit the way someone you've learned from sits: a teacher, a grandparent, a coach. Let your shoulders, hands and face borrow a little of their calm.
Breathe like that for a while, and notice what of them has already rubbed off on you.

wordCard.voice: We cannot but speak. Peter and John's answer when ordered to be silent: they can't help telling what they've seen and heard.

orig.note: Greek: boldness, open and frank speech. what the council saw in Peter and John in Acts 4:13.

carryVoice: Keep this: they had been with Jesus, and people could tell without being told. Day seven in Acts.
